title: CAP Theorem
used_in: Every distributed database — Cassandra, DynamoDB, Spanner, MongoDB.

payload.text: CAP is the most quoted — and most misunderstood — theorem in distributed systems. Eric Brewer conjectured in 2000, Gilbert and Lynch proved in 2002, that a distributed system can provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. The practical takeaway is sharper than the slogan: because partitions are inevitable on real networks, you are really choosing between C and A when a partition occurs. You cannot have all three.

payload.title: Definitions (precisely)
payload.body: Consistency (linearizability): every read sees the most recent write, as if there were a single copy. Availability: every non-failed node returns a response (not an error) for every request. Partition tolerance: the system continues to operate despite network partitions (dropped or delayed messages between nodes).

payload.ascii:
C
                   / \
                  /   \
                 /     \
                /  CP   \
               /         \
              /    AP     \
             /             \
            A---------------P

  CP: Consistency + Partition tolerance
      -> reject requests during partition (sacrifice A)
      -> e.g., Spanner, HBase, MongoDB (with majority write concern)

  AP: Availability + Partition tolerance
      -> serve stale data during partition (sacrifice C)
      -> e.g., Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB

  CA: Consistency + Availability
      -> only possible when there are no partitions
      -> e.g., a single-machine database (PostgreSQL on one box)
payload.caption: CAP triangle. Because partitions are inevitable, real distributed systems are CP or AP.
payload.voice_alt_text: A triangle diagram showing the three CAP properties at the corners. CP systems prioritize consistency and partition tolerance by rejecting requests during a partition. AP systems prioritize availability and partition tolerance by serving possibly stale data. CA systems only work without partitions, which means single-machine databases.

payload.text: The common framing 'pick two' is misleading because Partition tolerance is not optional on a real network — partitions will happen, and your system must handle them. So the real choice is: when a partition occurs, do you (a) refuse to serve requests you cannot prove are correct (CP — sacrifice availability), or (b) serve requests with the data you have, accepting it may be stale (AP — sacrifice strong consistency)? Both are valid; the choice depends on the workload.

payload.title: Common misconception
payload.body: CAP does NOT say 'you cannot have consistency and availability at the same time.' It says you cannot have both during a partition. When the network is healthy (no partition), a well-designed system can be both strongly consistent and highly available. PACELC is a more precise formulation: if there is a Partition (P), choose between A and C; Else (E), choose between L (latency) and C.

payload.text: CP systems: Google Spanner, HBase, MongoDB with majority write concern, any system using synchronous replication with quorum. They reject writes during partition rather than risk divergence. AP systems: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, Riak — they accept writes on any reachable node and reconcile later (eventual consistency). CA systems: a single PostgreSQL instance. Not distributed, so no partition to tolerate — but also no fault tolerance.

payload.question: What does CAP theorem actually guarantee about a distributed system?
options: You can always choose two of three: C, A, P.
During a network partition, you must choose between consistency and availability.
Strong consistency is impossible in distributed systems.
Availability is impossible in distributed systems.
payload.rationale: The 'pick two' framing is misleading because partitions are inevitable on real networks — P is not optional. The real guarantee is: during a partition, you cannot have both C and A. You either reject requests (CP) or serve possibly-stale data (AP). When there is no partition, you can have both. PACELC extends this: even without partition, you choose between latency and consistency on every write.

payload.question: You are designing a social media feed storage. Writes are user posts; reads are feed fetches. Which CAP trade-off makes sense?
options: CP — feeds must always show the latest post.
AP — a slightly stale feed is fine; the system must stay up during partitions.
All three are achievable with modern databases.
payload.rationale: Social media feeds tolerate staleness well — a user seeing a post 5 seconds late is not a problem. But the system being down during a partition is a major business problem. AP (eventual consistency) is the right choice: accept writes on any node, reconcile via read-repair or anti-entropy. This is why Cassandra and DynamoDB are popular for social feed storage. Note: some subsets (like payment state) might warrant CP — mixed systems are common.

pros: Gives a clear vocabulary for the consistency-availability trade-off.
Helps you choose the right database class for each workload.
Forces explicit reasoning about partition behavior.
cons: Frequently misquoted as 'pick two' when P is not optional.
Binary C vs A is too coarse — real systems are tunable (quorum sizes, consistency levels).
Does not address latency, which is often the real cost of strong consistency.

common_mistakes: Quoting CAP as 'pick two of three' without acknowledging partitions are inevitable.
Assuming 'eventual consistency' means 'eventually correct' — it means eventually converged, which can still be wrong.
Choosing AP for everything. Some data (payments, inventory) demands CP.
Forgetting that CAP is about partition behavior, not normal operation.
where_you_see_it: Every distributed database — Cassandra (AP), Spanner (CP), DynamoDB (AP), MongoDB (configurable).
Microservice architectures face the same trade-off when services cannot reach each other.
The NO CAP app itself: D1 is CP (single region, SQLite), Workers KV is AP (eventual consistency across regions).
interview_prompts: Explain CAP theorem. What does it really say?
Design a distributed counter (likes on a post). CP or AP? Why?
Your bank's ledger system must never lose a transaction. CP or AP? What are the implications?
PACELC extends CAP. Explain the difference.
summary: CAP is the most quoted — and most misunderstood — theorem in distributed systems. A distributed system can provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.
why_it_matters: Because partitions are inevitable on real networks, the real choice is between consistency and availability when a partition occurs. This trade-off shapes every distributed database design.
failure_modes: Split-brain — network partition causes two primaries, divergent writes, data loss on heal.
Stale reads — AP system serves outdated data that violates business invariants.
Write unavailability — CP system rejects writes during partition, blocking users.

real_system_mappings.how: AP system — accepts writes on any reachable node, reconciles via read-repair and anti-entropy.
CP system — synchronous replication with Paxos consensus, rejects writes during partition.
